source_caption:
The Sopranos changed television by making its main character someone audiences couldn’t easily root for—or look away from.

Tony Soprano was a mob boss dealing with panic attacks, family problems, and therapy. The show gave that complicated story room to unfold over seasons, helping make darker, more character-driven dramas feel possible on TV.

There are some great behind-the-scenes details, too. David Chase first imagined the story as a movie about a mobster and his mother. Fox passed on the series, and the version Chase pitched there didn’t even include murders. HBO gave him more freedom. Livia Soprano was partly based on Chase’s own mother, and she was originally supposed to die in the first episode—but Chase changed his mind.

It’s hard to imagine modern television without The Sopranos. What’s your favorite moment from the show?

source_details.synopsis: The Sopranos is an American crime drama television series created by David Chase for HBO. The series follows Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini), a New Jersey Mafia boss. Suffering from panic attacks, he reluctantly begins seeing psychiatrist Dr. Jennifer Melfi (Lorraine Bracco), who encourages him to open up about his difficulties balancing his family life with his criminal activities. Other important characters include Tony's family, Mafia colleagues, and rivals, most notably his wife Carmela (Edie Falco), his nephew and protégé Christopher Moltisanti (Michael Imperioli), and his uncle Corrado "Junior" Soprano (Dominic Chianese). Greenlit in 1997, the series was broadcast on HBO from January 1
